title: Νέστωρ ἀριστῆας ἐγείρει
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Nestor answers Agamemnon’s plan with a promise to follow and a list of men to rouse: Diomedes, Odysseus, the two Ajaxes, the son of Phyleus and Idomeneus. He would rebuke Menelaus for sleeping, but Agamemnon says his brother woke first and has already been sent to call the others. Nestor dresses, goes along the ships, and wakes Odysseus with a call; the two find Diomedes asleep on an oxhide among his sleeping companions, and Nestor kicks him awake. Diomedes complains that younger men might do this, and Nestor answers that the Achaeans stand on a razor’s edge and sends him to fetch the other two. Diomedes puts on a lion skin and goes; the party finds the guards awake, as sleepless as dogs that have heard a wild beast, and Nestor, glad of the sight, tells them to keep watch lest the enemy have joy of them.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The reply formula, as in the Odyssey and earlier in the Iliad: τόν ‘him’ is Agamemnon, whose proposal ended the last part, ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, ἔπειτα ‘then’. Nestor’s name-epithet is Γερήνιος ἱππότα, ‘the Gerenian horseman’: ἱππότα is an old nominative in -ᾱ (= ἱππότης), and the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (a place, Gerenia, or a word related to γέρων ‘old man’), so the English leaves it as a name. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
οὔ θην Ἕκτορι πάντα νοήματα μητίετα Ζεὺς
ἐκτελέει, ὅσα πού νυν ἐέλπεται·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste anax andrōn Agamemnon
ou thēn Hektori panta noēmata mētieta Zeus
ekteleei, hosa pou nyn eelpetai·
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, Zeus the counsellor will surely not bring all of Hector’s purposes to pass, all that he now hopes for;
sentences.n: Nestor begins by comforting Agamemnon. The first line is word for word the address that opens Nestor’s speech at 2.434; κύδιστε is the superlative of κυδρός ‘glorious’, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s title. οὔ θην ‘surely not’ governs ἐκτελέει, the uncontracted future of ἐκτελέω (= ἐκτελεῖ), ‘will bring to pass’. Its subject is μητίετα Ζεύς ‘Zeus the counsellor’, μητίετα being an old nominative in -α like ἱππότα; the object πάντα νοήματα ‘all the thoughts’ stands before it, with Ἕκτορι ‘for Hector’ in the dative of interest. ὅσα πού νυν ἐέλπεται is ‘as many as he now, I suppose, hopes’: ἐέλπεται is ἔλπεται with its first vowel lengthened, and Hector is its subject.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μιν οἴω
κήδεσι μοχθήσειν καὶ πλείοσιν, εἴ κεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐκ χόλου ἀργαλέοιο μεταστρέψῃ φίλον ἦτορ.
sentences.tr:
alla min oiō
kēdesi mochthēsein kai pleiosin, ei ken Achilleus
ek cholou argaleoio metastrepsēi philon ētor.
sentences.l:
but him I think
with troubles will toil, and more of them, if Achilles
out of grievous anger should turn his dear heart round.
sentences.i: but I think he will labour under troubles, and still more of them, if Achilles turns his dear heart round from its grievous anger.
sentences.n: ἀλλά μιν οἴω: μιν is Hector, and οἴω (= οἴομαι) ‘I think’ takes the future infinitive μοχθήσειν ‘will toil’, from μοχθέω ‘labour, suffer hardship’. κήδεσι is a dative of κῆδος ‘trouble, care’, ‘with troubles’, and καὶ πλείοσιν ‘and more of them’ adds that the troubles will grow. εἴ κεν with the subjunctive μεταστρέψῃ looks forward: ‘if Achilles should turn round’; μεταστρέφω is ‘turn about, change’, its object is φίλον ἦτορ ‘dear heart’, and ἐκ χόλου ἀργαλέοιο ‘out of grievous anger’ (epic genitive -οιο) says what he turns away from. χόλος is ‘anger’, apart from μῆνις ‘wrath’.

sentences.t: σοὶ δὲ μάλ’ ἕψομ’ ἐγώ·
sentences.tr: soi de mal’ hepsom’ egō·
sentences.l: And you, very much, will I follow, I;
sentences.i: And I will most certainly follow you;
sentences.n: ἕψομ’ is ἕψομαι, the future of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, with its vowel elided and the dative σοί ‘you’ before it. μάλα ‘very much, indeed’ strengthens the promise, and ἐγώ ‘I’ is added for emphasis. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of the line, and the rest of the line opens the next unit.

sentences.t:
ποτὶ δ’ αὖ καὶ ἐγείρομεν ἄλλους
ἠμὲν Τυδεΐδην δουρὶ κλυτὸν ἠδ’ Ὀδυσῆα
ἠδ’ Αἴαντα ταχὺν καὶ Φυλέος ἄλκιμον υἱόν.
sentences.tr:
poti d’ au kai egeiromen allous
ēmen Tydeïdēn douri klyton ēd’ Odysēa
ēd’ Aianta tachyn kai Phyleos alkimon huion.
sentences.l:
and besides, in turn, let us also rouse others,
both the son of Tydeus, famed with the spear, and Odysseus,
and swift Ajax and the sturdy son of Phyleus.
sentences.i: and let us also rouse others besides: both the son of Tydeus, famed for his spear, and Odysseus, and swift Ajax and the sturdy son of Phyleus.
sentences.n: ποτί is the epic form of πρός, here an adverb ‘besides’, and αὖ is ‘in turn, moreover’; ἐγείρομεν is a subjunctive with a short vowel, ‘let us rouse’. The others are listed with ἠμέν … ἠδ’ … ἠδ’ ‘both … and … and’: Τυδεΐδην ‘the son of Tydeus’ (Diomedes, whom line 150 names), δουρὶ κλυτόν ‘famed with the spear’ (a dative of respect), Ὀδυσῆα with the epic -η-, Αἴαντα ταχύν ‘swift Ajax’, and Φυλέος … υἱόν ‘the son of Phyleus’, Φυλέος being an epic genitive. ἄλκιμος is ‘sturdy’. The son of Phyleus is not named here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴ τις καὶ τούσδε μετοιχόμενος καλέσειεν
ἀντίθεόν τ’ Αἴαντα καὶ Ἰδομενῆα ἄνακτα·
sentences.tr:
all’ ei tis kai tousde metoichomenos kaleseien
antitheon t’ Aianta kai Idomenēa anakta·
sentences.l:
But if some one these also, going after them, would call,
godlike Ajax and lord Idomeneus;
sentences.i: But if only someone would go after these too and call them, godlike Ajax and lord Idomeneus;
sentences.n: εἰ with the optative καλέσειεν, standing alone, is a wish: ‘if only someone would call’. μετοίχομαι is ‘go after, go among’, and τούσδε ‘these here’ is picked up by the two names that follow, ἀντίθεον … Αἴαντα ‘godlike Ajax’ and Ἰδομενῆα ἄνακτα ‘lord Idomeneus’ (epic -η-). A second Ajax appears here; the first, at line 110, was ‘swift’, and the lines give a father’s name for neither. At 10.53 Agamemnon had told Menelaus to call these two, and the wish is that someone go to them now.

sentences.t: τῶν γὰρ νῆες ἔασιν ἑκαστάτω, οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἐγγύς.
sentences.tr: tōn gar nēes easin hekastatō, oude mal’ engys.
sentences.l: for their ships are farthest away, and not at all near.
sentences.i: for their ships lie farthest off, and not at all close.
sentences.n: τῶν γάρ gives the reason for the wish: ‘for their ships…’. ἔασιν is the epic third plural of εἰμί (= εἰσίν). ἑκαστάτω is an adverb of the superlative, ‘farthest’, built on ἑκάς ‘far’; οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἐγγύς is ‘and not at all near’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ φίλον περ ἐόντα καὶ αἰδοῖον Μενέλαον
νεικέσω, εἴ πέρ μοι νεμεσήσεαι, οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω
ὡς εὕδει, σοὶ δ’ οἴῳ ἐπέτρεψεν πονέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
alla philon per eonta kai aidoion Menelaon
neikesō, ei per moi nemesēseai, oud’ epikeusō
hōs heudei, soi d’ oiōi epetrepsen poneesthai.
sentences.l:
But Menelaus, dear though he is and revered,
I will revile, even if you will feel resentment at me, and I will not hide
that he sleeps, and to you alone has entrusted the toiling.
sentences.i: But Menelaus, dear though he is and revered, I will revile, even if you feel resentment at me, and I will not hide that he sleeps and has left the toil to you alone.
sentences.n: ἀλλά turns to a different man, Menelaus, who is named first and waits for his verb in the next line. φίλον περ ἐόντα καὶ αἰδοῖον ‘dear though he is and revered’: περ with a participle is concessive, and αἰδοῖος is ‘revered’. νεικέσω is a short-vowel subjunctive of νεικέω ‘revile’, a strong word for scolding, and the English keeps ‘revile’ for it everywhere. εἴ πέρ μοι νεμεσήσεαι is ‘even if you will feel resentment at me’, the uncontracted future middle of νεμεσάω (= νεμεσήσῃ) with the dative; οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω ‘nor will I hide’ is from ἐπικεύθω. ὡς εὕδει ‘that he sleeps’; σοὶ δ’ οἴῳ ‘and to you alone’, ἐπέτρεψεν the aorist of ἐπιτρέπω ‘entrust, leave to’, with the uncontracted infinitive πονέεσθαι ‘to toil’ (= πονεῖσθαι).

sentences.t:
νῦν ὄφελεν κατὰ πάντας ἀριστῆας πονέεσθαι
λισσόμενος· χρειὼ γὰρ ἱκάνεται οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτός.
sentences.tr:
nyn ophelen kata pantas aristēas poneesthai
lissomenos· chreiō gar hikanetai ouket’ anektos.
sentences.l:
Now he ought to toil among all the best men,
beseeching; for a need is coming that is no longer bearable.”
sentences.i: Now he ought to be going about among all the best men, entreating them; for a need is coming that can no longer be borne.”
sentences.n: ὄφελεν is the aorist of ὀφείλω ‘owe, ought’ (the verb of αἴθ’ ὄφελες ‘would that’), ‘he ought’, said of what Menelaus is not doing. κατὰ πάντας ἀριστῆας ‘among all the best men’, with the participle λισσόμενος ‘beseeching’ (λίσσομαι) and πονέεσθαι ‘to toil’ again. χρειώ ‘need’ is a feminine noun in -ώ and the subject of ἱκάνεται ‘comes upon’; ἀνεκτός ‘bearable’ is an adjective of two endings, so its masculine form stands with the feminine noun, and οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτός is ‘no longer bearable’. Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Nestor’s speech ended at 118, and the edition begins a new paragraph with Agamemnon’s answer. The line is the formula for a speaker who answers in turn: τόν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘him’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπεν the Homeric form of ‘addressed’ (Attic προσεῖπεν). The English keeps it apart from ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, a different formula. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock title. The same line stands at 9.114.

sentences.t: ὦ γέρον ἄλλοτε μέν σε καὶ αἰτιάασθαι ἄνωγα·
sentences.tr: ō geron allote men se kai aitiaasthai anōga·
sentences.l: “Old man, at other times, indeed, you also to blame I bid;
sentences.i: “Old man, at other times I even bid you find fault;
sentences.n: Agamemnon does not agree that Menelaus is to be blamed now. ὦ γέρον ‘Old man’ is the polite address to an elder. ἄλλοτε μέν ‘at other times’ is answered by νῦν δέ ‘but now’ in line 124. αἰτιάασθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of αἰτιάομαι ‘blame’ (= αἰτιᾶσθαι), depending on ἄνωγα, a perfect with the sense of a present, ‘I bid’. The person to be blamed is not named in this line; line 121 shows that it is Menelaus.

sentences.t:
πολλάκι γὰρ μεθιεῖ τε καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλει πονέεσθαι
οὔτ’ ὄκνῳ εἴκων οὔτ’ ἀφραδίῃσι νόοιο,
ἀλλ’ ἐμέ τ’ εἰσορόων καὶ ἐμὴν ποτιδέγμενος ὁρμήν.
sentences.tr:
pollaki gar methiei te kai ouk ethelei poneesthai
out’ oknōi eikōn out’ aphradiēisi nooio,
all’ eme t’ eisoroōn kai emēn potidegmenos hormēn.
sentences.i: for he often slackens and will not toil, not because he gives way to hesitation or to folly of mind, but because he looks to me and waits for my impulse.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for ‘at other times’. πολλάκι is πολλάκις ‘often’; μεθιεῖ is the present of μεθίημι ‘slacken, let go’; οὐκ ἐθέλει ‘he is not willing’. οὔτε … οὔτε lists what the slackness is not due to: ὄκνῳ ‘hesitation’, with εἴκων ‘yielding’, and ἀφραδίῃσι ‘follies, thoughtlessness’ (a plural noun), with νόοιο, the epic genitive of νόος ‘mind’. ἀλλά brings the true reason: εἰσορόων is the uncontracted participle of εἰσοράω ‘look to’ (= εἰσορῶν), ποτιδέγμενος ‘waiting for’ is ποτί (= πρός) with a participle of δέχομαι, and ὁρμή is a start or impulse, ‘my move’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἐμέο πρότερος μάλ’ ἐπέγρετο καί μοι ἐπέστη·
sentences.tr: nyn d’ emeo proteros mal’ epegreto kai moi epestē·
sentences.l: But now, earlier than I, very much, he woke up and stood over me;
sentences.i: But now he woke much sooner than I did, and stood beside me;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ answers ἄλλοτε μέν of line 120. ἐμέο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, used after the comparative πρότερος ‘earlier’, ‘earlier than I’, and μάλα strengthens it. ἐπέγρετο is an aorist middle of ἐγείρω with ἐπί, ‘woke up’; καί μοι ἐπέστη ‘and stood over me’ is the aorist of ἐφίστημι with the dative of the person.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ προέηκα καλήμεναι οὓς σὺ μεταλλᾷς.
sentences.tr: ton men egō proeēka kalēmenai hous sy metallāis.
sentences.l: Him I sent forth to call those whom you ask after.
sentences.i: I sent him off to call the men you are asking after.
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἐγώ: τόν is Menelaus, ‘him’, put first, and προέηκα is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forward’. καλήμεναι is the epic infinitive of καλέω (= καλεῖν), here of purpose, ‘to call’. οὓς σὺ μεταλλᾷς ‘those whom you ask after’: μεταλλάω is ‘inquire after, search out’, and the contracted form μεταλλᾷς stands for μεταλλάεις. The men are those Nestor has just named.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν·
sentences.tr: all’ iomen·
sentences.l: But let us go;
sentences.i: But come, let us go;
sentences.n: ἴομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive of εἶμι ‘go’ (= ἴωμεν), ‘let us go’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
κείνους δὲ κιχησόμεθα πρὸ πυλάων
ἐν φυλάκεσσ’, ἵνα γάρ σφιν ἐπέφραδον ἠγερέθεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
keinous de kichēsometha pro pylaōn
en phylakess’, hina gar sphin epephradon ēgerethesthai.
sentences.l:
and those we shall find before the gates
among the guards, for there I told them to assemble.”
sentences.i: and we shall find them in front of the gates among the guards, for that is where I told them to gather.”
sentences.n: κείνους is the epic form of ἐκείνους ‘those’. κιχησόμεθα is the future middle of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’, formed on the stem κιχη-. πρὸ πυλάων ‘in front of the gates’ has the epic genitive plural -άων, and ἐν φυλάκεσσ’ ‘among the guards’ the dative -εσσι. ἵνα γάρ: ἵνα is ‘where’, and γάρ gives the reason; σφιν is ‘to them’, ἐπέφραδον the aorist of φράζω ‘tell, point out’, and ἠγερέθεσθαι an epic infinitive of ἠγερέθομαι ‘assemble’. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at 102, with the edition’s paragraph break: Nestor answers Agamemnon. τόν ‘him’ is Agamemnon, ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, and Γερήνιος ἱππότα is Nestor’s name-epithet, ‘the Gerenian horseman’, left as a name because the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed.

sentences.t:
οὕτως οὔ τίς οἱ νεμεσήσεται οὐδ’ ἀπιθήσει
Ἀργείων, ὅτε κέν τιν’ ἐποτρύνῃ καὶ ἀνώγῃ.
sentences.tr:
houtōs ou tis hoi nemesēsetai oud’ apithēsei
Argeiōn, hote ken tin’ epotrynēi kai anōgēi.
sentences.l:
“Thus no one will feel resentment at him, nor disobey,
of the Argives, whenever he urges on and bids anyone.”
sentences.i: “In that case none of the Argives will feel resentment at him or disobey him, whenever he urges anyone on or gives an order.”
sentences.n: οὕτως ‘in this way’: since Menelaus has been sent by Agamemnon himself, nobody will object. οὔ τίς οἱ νεμεσήσεται ‘no one will feel resentment at him’, with the dative οἱ and the future middle of νεμεσάω as in line 115; οὐδ’ ἀπιθήσει ‘nor will he disobey’ is the future of ἀπιθέω, the negative of πείθομαι ‘obey’. Ἀργείων ‘of the Argives’ stands first in the next line, as the partitive genitive after οὔ τίς. ὅτε κέν τιν’ ἐποτρύνῃ καὶ ἀνώγῃ ‘whenever he urges anyone on and bids him’: ὅτε κεν with the subjunctive is general, ἐποτρύνω is ‘urge on’, and ἀνώγῃ is the subjunctive of ἄνωγα ‘bid’. Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἔνδυνε περὶ στήθεσσι χιτῶνα,
ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρα χλαῖναν περονήσατο φοινικόεσσαν
διπλῆν ἐκταδίην, οὔλη δ’ ἐπενήνοθε λάχνη.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn endyne peri stēthessi chitōna,
possi d’ hypo liparoisin edēsato kala pedila,
amphi d’ ara chlainan peronēsato phoinikoessan
diplēn ektadiēn, oulē d’ epenēnothe lachnē.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he put on about his chest the tunic,
and under his sleek feet he bound fine sandals,
and about him then he pinned a cloak, a crimson one,
double, outstretched, and a thick nap was upon it.
sentences.i: So he spoke, put the tunic on over his chest, bound fine sandals beneath his sleek feet, and pinned about him a crimson cloak, double and ample, with a thick nap on it.
sentences.n: Nestor dresses in stages, as Agamemnon did at 21–24. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ has Nestor as its subject; ἔνδυνε ‘put on’ is the imperfect of ἐνδύνω, with περὶ στήθεσσι ‘about his chest’. Line 132 stands word for word at 2.44. ἀμφὶ … περονήσατο is a tmesis: περονάομαι is ‘fasten with a pin’ (περόνη), so ‘pinned about himself’. χλαῖναν φοινικόεσσαν is ‘a crimson cloak’ (the feminine accusative in -εσσαν); διπλῆν ‘double’ means folded in two. ἐκταδίην is formed on ἐκτείνω ‘stretch out’ and means ‘stretched out’; said of a cloak, the likely sense is ‘full, ample’, which the English takes. οὔλη … λάχνη ‘a thick nap’: οὖλος is ‘thick’, and λάχνη is woolly hair, here the nap of the cloth; ἐπενήνοθε is an old perfect of a verb whose root is not clear, usually taken as ‘lies upon, grows upon’.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος ἀκαχμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι κατὰ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων.
sentences.tr:
heileto d’ alkimon enchos akachmenon oxeï chalkōi,
bē d’ ienai kata nēas Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn.
sentences.l:
and he took up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze,
and set out to go along the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans.
sentences.i: He took up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze, and set out along the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans.
sentences.n: Line 135 stands also in the Odyssey, where Telemachus takes up his spear, and the English is kept. εἵλετο ‘took up’, ἄλκιμον ‘sturdy’, ἀκαχμένον a perfect passive participle of an old verb meaning ‘point’ (from the root of ἀκωκή ‘point’), ‘pointed’, with ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘sharp bronze’; the edition prints the diaeresis. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is ‘set out to go’ (βῆ the aorist of βαίνω, ἰέναι the infinitive of εἶμι), and κατὰ νῆας ‘along the ships’. Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων ‘of the bronze-shirted Achaeans’ is a stock phrase, χαλκοχιτώνων being built on χαλκός ‘bronze’ and χιτών ‘tunic’.

sentences.t:
πρῶτον ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντον
ἐξ ὕπνου ἀνέγειρε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ
φθεγξάμενος·
sentences.tr:
prōton epeit’ Odysēa Dii mētin atalanton
ex hypnou anegeire Gerēnios hippota Nestōr
phthenxamenos·
sentences.i: First the Gerenian horseman Nestor woke Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in cunning, from sleep, calling out;
sentences.n: πρῶτον … ἔπειτα ‘first, then’ opens the waking of the chiefs in order. Ὀδυσῆα Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντον ‘Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in cunning’ is a phrase that also stands at 2.169: ἀτάλαντος ‘equal’ takes the dative Διί, and μῆτιν is an accusative of respect, ‘in cunning’. ἐξ ὕπνου ἀνέγειρε ‘woke from sleep’, with Nestor’s name-epithet as subject. φθεγξάμενος is the aorist participle of φθέγγομαι ‘raise one’s voice, call out’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 139.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ αἶψα περὶ φρένας ἤλυθ’ ἰωή,
ἐκ δ’ ἦλθε κλισίης καί σφεας πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ aipsa peri phrenas ēlyth’ iōē,
ek d’ ēlthe klisiēs kai spheas pros mython eeipe·
sentences.l:
and him at once round his wits came the call,
and out of his hut he came, and to them a word he spoke:
sentences.i: and the call at once pervaded his wits, and he came out of his hut and spoke a word to them:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αἶψα: τόν is Odysseus, and αἶψα ‘at once’. περὶ φρένας ἤλυθ’ ‘came about his wits’ uses περί with the accusative, so that the sound goes all round and through them; ἤλυθε is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι and ἰωή is a ‘cry, call’. ἐκ δ’ ἦλθε κλισίης ‘and out of his hut he came’, with the genitive of the place left (κλισίη ‘hut’). In καί σφεας πρὸς … ἔειπε the preposition is separated from its verb (tmesis), ‘spoke to them’: σφεας is ‘them’, ἔειπε the epic aorist of εἶπον, and μῦθον ‘word’ is its object. The unit begins in the middle of line 139, after the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τίφθ’ οὕτω κατὰ νῆας ἀνὰ στρατὸν οἶοι ἀλᾶσθε
νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην, ὅ τι δὴ χρειὼ τόσον ἵκει;
sentences.tr:
tiphth’ houtō kata nēas ana straton oioi alasthe
nykta di’ ambrosiēn, ho ti dē chreiō toson hikei;
sentences.l:
“Why ever thus along the ships, up through the army, do you wander alone
through the ambrosial night, that need indeed so greatly comes?”
sentences.i: “Why do you wander alone like this along the ships and through the army, through the ambrosial night? Is it that so great a need has come?”
sentences.n: Odysseus’ first words are a question. τίφθ’ is an elided variant of the epic τίπτε (τί ποτε), ‘why ever’. οἶοι ‘alone’ is plural, like ἀλᾶσθε ‘you wander’, the second plural of ἀλάομαι: the two men are spoken of with plural, not dual, forms. κατὰ νῆας ἀνὰ στρατόν ‘along the ships, up through the army’. νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην ‘through the ambrosial night’ has the preposition between its accusative noun and the adjective ἀμβρόσιος, rendered ‘ambrosial’. ὅ τι δὴ χρειὼ τόσον ἵκει: ὅ τι is neuter and χρειώ feminine, so it cannot be ‘what’ qualifying the need (and τόσον is an adverb, ‘so greatly’); it is ὅτι ‘that’, and the clause asks whether so great a need ‘comes’, ἵκει being the present of ἵκω ‘come’. The question ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at 102 and 128: Odysseus has asked a question, and Nestor answers him. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ
μὴ νεμέσα·
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē polymēchan’ Odysseu
mē nemesa·
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
do not feel resentment;
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, do not feel resentment;
sentences.n: The address to Odysseus is the one Athena used at 2.173. διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’, Λαερτιάδη ‘son of Laertes’ (the vocative of a patronymic), and πολυμήχαν’ ‘of many devices’ with its vowel dropped before Ὀδυσσεῦ. μὴ νεμέσα is a prohibition with the present imperative of νεμεσάω ‘feel resentment’, the verb of lines 115 and 129. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 145.

sentences.t: τοῖον γὰρ ἄχος βεβίηκεν Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr: toion gar achos bebiēken Achaious.
sentences.l: for such grief has come upon the Achaeans.
sentences.i: for such grief has come upon the Achaeans.
sentences.n: τοῖον ‘such’ and ἄχος ‘grief’ give the reason. βεβίηκεν is a perfect whose origin is not certain, from βιβάω ‘stride’ or from βία ‘force’; with the accusative Ἀχαιούς it means ‘has come upon, has pressed hard on’, which suits either. The same verb recurs at 172.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἕπε’, ὄφρα καὶ ἄλλον ἐγείρομεν ὅν τ’ ἐπέοικε
βουλὰς βουλεύειν, ἢ φευγέμεν ἠὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
all’ hepe’, ophra kai allon egeiromen hon t’ epeoike
boulas bouleuein, ē pheugemen ēe machesthai.
sentences.l:
But follow, so that we may rouse another too, one whom it is fitting
to plan plans, whether to flee or to fight.”
sentences.i: But follow, so that we may rouse another man as well, one whose place it is to take counsel on whether to flee or to fight.”
sentences.n: ἕπε’ is ἕπεο, the imperative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, elided. ὄφρα … ἐγείρομεν ‘so that we may rouse’ is a purpose clause with a short-vowel subjunctive. ἄλλον ὅν τ’ ἐπέοικε ‘another, one whom it is fitting’: the relative has epic τε, and ἐπέοικε is a perfect with present sense, ‘it befits’. βουλὰς βουλεύειν ‘to plan plans’ repeats one root in verb and noun; ἢ φευγέμεν ἠὲ μάχεσθαι ‘whether to flee or to fight’, with φευγέμεν the epic infinitive (= φεύγειν). Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δὲ κλισίην δὲ κιὼν πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεὺς
ποικίλον ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι σάκος θέτο, βῆ δὲ μετ’ αὐτούς.
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho de klisiēn de kiōn polymētis Odysseus
poikilon amph’ ōmoisi sakos theto, bē de met’ autous.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he, to his hut going, many-wiled Odysseus,
an intricate shield about his shoulders put, and went after them.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Odysseus of many wiles went to his hut, put an intricate shield about his shoulders, and set out after them.
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ’ is ὣς φάτο, with the final vowel elided and the τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ὃ δέ ‘and he’, Odysseus. κλισίην δέ ‘to his hut’ has the suffix -δε of direction, and κιών is the participle of κίω ‘go’. πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς ‘Odysseus of many wiles’ is the stock epithet. ποικίλον ‘intricate’ covers things of varied colour or elaborate work; σάκος is ‘shield’. ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι ‘about his shoulders’ (epic dative -οισι); θέτο is the aorist middle of τίθημι, ‘put on himself’. βῆ δὲ μετ’ αὐτούς ‘and went after them’, μετά with the accusative of persons meaning ‘in the track of’.

sentences.t: βὰν δ’ ἐπὶ Τυδεΐδην Διομήδεα·
sentences.tr: ban d’ epi Tydeïdēn Diomēdea·
sentences.l: And they went to Tydeus’-son Diomedes;
sentences.i: And they went to Diomedes, son of Tydeus;
sentences.n: βάν is the unaugmented third plural aorist of βαίνω, ‘they went’ (Nestor and Odysseus). ἐπὶ … Διομήδεα ‘to Diomedes’, with ἐπί and the accusative of the person approached; Τυδεΐδην is the patronymic ‘son of Tydeus’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 150.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ κίχανον
ἐκτὸς ἀπὸ κλισίης σὺν τεύχεσιν·
sentences.tr:
ton de kichanon
ektos apo klisiēs syn teuchesin·
sentences.l:
and him they came upon
outside, away from the hut, with armour;
sentences.i: and they found him outside his hut with his armour;
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ κίχανον ‘and they came upon him’: κίχανον is an unaugmented past tense of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’. ἐκτὸς ἀπὸ κλισίης ‘outside, away from the hut’, and σὺν τεύχεσιν ‘with armour’, the dative plural of τεύχεα; the English supplies ‘his’. The unit begins in the middle of line 150 and ends at the raised dot (·) in line 151.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι
εὗδον, ὑπὸ κρασὶν δ’ ἔχον ἀσπίδας·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ hetairoi
heudon, hypo krasin d’ echon aspidas·
sentences.l:
and about him his companions
were sleeping, and under their heads they had shields;
sentences.i: and around him his companions were sleeping, with their shields under their heads;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι: ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘around’ him, and ἑταῖροι ‘companions’. εὗδον is the imperfect of εὕδω ‘sleep’. ὑπὸ κρασὶν δ’ ἔχον ἀσπίδας ‘and under their heads they had shields’: κράς ‘head’ has the dative plural κρασί, and the shields served as pillows. The unit begins in the middle of line 151 and ends at the raised dot (·) in line 152.

sentences.t:
ἔγχεα δέ σφιν
ὄρθ’ ἐπὶ σαυρωτῆρος ἐλήλατο, τῆλε δὲ χαλκὸς
λάμφ’ ὥς τε στεροπὴ πατρὸς Διός·
sentences.tr:
enchea de sphin
orth’ epi saurōtēros elēlato, tēle de chalkos
lamph’ hōs te steropē patros Dios·
sentences.i: their spears stood upright, driven in on the butt-spike, and the bronze shone far off like the lightning of father Zeus;
sentences.n: σφιν is ‘to them’, a dative of possession, so ‘their spears’. ὄρθ’ ἐπὶ σαυρωτῆρος ‘upright on the butt-spike’: the σαυρωτήρ is the spike at the butt end of the shaft, which lets the spear be set in the ground. ἐλήλατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, ‘had been driven in’. τῆλε ‘far off’; λάμφ’ is ἔλαμπε unaugmented and elided, the imperfect of λάμπω. ὥς τε στεροπή ‘like lightning’, with πατρὸς Διός ‘of father Zeus’. The unit begins in the middle of line 152 and ends at the raised dot (·) in line 154.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως
εὗδ’, ὑπὸ δ’ ἔστρωτο ῥινὸν βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο,
αὐτὰρ ὑπὸ κράτεσφι τάπης τετάνυστο φαεινός.
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ hērōs
heud’, hypo d’ estrōto rhinon boos agrauloio,
autar hypo kratesphi tapēs tetanysto phaeinos.
sentences.l:
but he himself, the hero,
was sleeping, and under him he had spread the hide of a field-dwelling ox,
and under his head a rug was stretched, shining.
sentences.i: but the hero himself lay sleeping, with the hide of an ox that lives in the fields spread under him, and under his head a shining rug was stretched.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως ‘but he, the hero’ is Diomedes; ἥρως is a title. εὗδε is the imperfect of εὕδω. ἔστρωτο is the pluperfect of στρώννυμι ‘spread’; since ῥινόν ‘hide’ is an accusative, the verb is middle and Diomedes is its subject, ‘he had spread under himself’, so that the hide lay spread beneath him. βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο ‘of a field-dwelling ox’: ἄγραυλος means ‘living in the fields’, with the epic genitive -οιο. κράτεσφι is the stem of κρατός ‘head’ with the ending -φι, ‘under his head’; τάπης is a ‘rug’, τετάνυστο the pluperfect passive of τανύω ‘stretch’, and φαεινός ‘shining’. The unit begins in the middle of line 154.

sentences.t:
τὸν παρστὰς ἀνέγειρε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ,
λὰξ ποδὶ κινήσας, ὄτρυνέ τε νείκεσέ τ’ ἄντην·
sentences.tr:
ton parstas anegeire Gerēnios hippota Nestōr,
lax podi kinēsas, otryne te neikese t’ antēn·
sentences.l:
Him, standing beside, awakened the Gerenian horseman Nestor,
having stirred him with a kick of the foot, and urged him on, and reviled him to his face:
sentences.i: Standing beside him, the Gerenian horseman Nestor woke him, stirring him with a kick of his foot, and urged him on and reviled him to his face:
sentences.n: παρστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’, and τόν ‘him’ is the object of ἀνέγειρε ‘woke’. Nestor’s name-epithet is the one used at 102. λὰξ ποδὶ κινήσας ‘having stirred him with a kick of the foot’: λάξ ‘with the heel’ is an adverb, and κινήσας the aorist participle of κινέω ‘move’. ὄτρυνέ τε νείκεσέ τ’ ‘urged him on and reviled him’ joins two aorists with τε … τε, ὄτρυνε being the unaugmented aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’ and νείκεσε that of νεικέω ‘revile’; ἄντην is ‘face to face’. The colon opens Nestor’s words.

sentences.t: ἔγρεο Τυδέος υἱέ·
sentences.tr: egreo Tydeos huie·
sentences.l: “Wake up, son of Tydeus;
sentences.i: “Wake up, son of Tydeus;
sentences.n: ἔγρεο is the imperative of the aorist middle of ἐγείρω, ‘wake up’. Τυδέος υἱέ is the vocative ‘son of Tydeus’, with the epic genitive Τυδέος. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 159.

sentences.t: τί πάννυχον ὕπνον ἀωτεῖς;
sentences.tr: ti pannychon hypnon aōteis;
sentences.l: why do you slumber the whole night’s sleep?
sentences.i: why are you slumbering the whole night through?
sentences.n: ἀωτέω is a rare verb for ‘sleep, slumber’, whose formation is not certain; the meaning is taken from the context. πάννυχον ὕπνον ‘a sleep all night long’ is a cognate accusative of ἀωτεῖς, with πάννυχος ‘all-night’ agreeing with ὕπνον. The question ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἀΐεις ὡς Τρῶες ἐπὶ θρωσμῷ πεδίοιο
εἵαται ἄγχι νεῶν, ὀλίγος δ’ ἔτι χῶρος ἐρύκει;
sentences.tr:
ouk aïeis hōs Trōes epi thrōsmōi pedioio
heiatai anchi neōn, oligos d’ eti chōros erykei;
sentences.l:
Do you not hear how the Trojans on the rising ground of the plain
are seated near the ships, and a little space still holds them off?”
sentences.i: Do you not hear how the Trojans are camped on the rising ground of the plain, close to the ships, and only a little space of ground still holds them off?”
sentences.n: οὐκ ἀΐεις ὡς ‘do you not perceive how’: ἀΐω is ‘perceive, hear’, the verb that returns as the optative ἀΐοιεν at 189. εἵαται is the epic third plural of ἧμαι ‘sit’, ‘are seated’, and so ‘are encamped’; ἄγχι νεῶν ‘near the ships’. ἐπὶ θρωσμῷ πεδίοιο ‘on the rising ground of the plain’: θρωσμός is a rise in the ground, from θρώσκω ‘leap’, and πεδίοιο the epic genitive of πεδίον. ὀλίγος δ’ ἔτι χῶρος ἐρύκει is ‘and only a little space still holds back’, the object ‘them’ being understood. Nestor’s speech ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δ’ ἐξ ὕπνοιο μάλα κραιπνῶς ἀνόρουσε,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho d’ ex hypnoio mala kraipnōs anorouse,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he out of sleep very swiftly sprang up,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Diomedes sprang up very swiftly out of sleep, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins. ὣς φάθ’ is ὣς φάτο, and ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is now Diomedes. ἐξ ὕπνοιο ‘out of sleep’ has the epic genitive -οιο; μάλα κραιπνῶς ‘very swiftly’; ἀνόρουσε is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘spring up’. Line 163 is the formula that stands at 1.201; μιν is Nestor here, so the English has ‘to him’. φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, προσηύδα ‘spoke to’.

sentences.t: σχέτλιός ἐσσι γεραιέ·
sentences.tr: schetlios essi geraie·
sentences.l: “Cruel you are, aged one;
sentences.i: “You are cruel, old man;
sentences.n: Diomedes answers Nestor’s reproach with one of his own. σχέτλιος is a word of complaint whose force varies, ‘hard, relentless’; here it is half in fondness, as in the vocative σχέτλιε ‘cruel one’ elsewhere, and the English keeps ‘cruel’. γεραιέ is the vocative of γεραιός ‘aged’, a respectful address. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 164.

sentences.t: σὺ μὲν πόνου οὔ ποτε λήγεις.
sentences.tr: sy men ponou ou pote lēgeis.
sentences.l: you, for your part, never cease from toil.
sentences.i: you never cease from toil.
sentences.n: σὺ μέν ‘you, for your part’ is answered by σὺ δέ in line 167. λήγω ‘cease’ takes the genitive of what one leaves off, so πόνου οὔ ποτε λήγεις is ‘you never cease from toil’.

sentences.l:
Are there not other, younger, sons of the Achaeans
who could then rouse each of the kings,
going about everywhere?
sentences.i: Are there not other sons of the Achaeans, younger than you, who could then go about everywhere and rouse each of the kings?
sentences.n: οὔ νυ … ; expects the answer ‘yes’: ‘are there not…?’. ἔασι is the epic third plural of εἰμί (= εἰσί), νεώτεροι ‘younger’, and υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘sons of the Achaeans’ means the young men of the army. οἵ κεν … ἐγείρειαν ‘who could rouse’ is a potential optative with κεν, ἔπειτα ‘then, in that case’, and ἕκαστον … βασιλήων ‘each of the kings’ has a partitive genitive. ἐποιχόμενοι is the participle of ἐποίχομαι ‘go about to’, and πάντῃ ‘everywhere’. The question ends at the Greek question mark, in the middle of line 167.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ ἀμήχανός ἐσσι γεραιέ.
sentences.tr: sy d’ amēchanos essi geraie.
sentences.l: but you are past all dealing with, aged one.”
sentences.i: but you are impossible to deal with, old man.”
sentences.n: ἀμήχανος is ‘without resource’, said of a person with whom nothing can be done, ‘one who cannot be dealt with’. Where the Odyssey uses it of a person it is ‘helpless’, which would say that Nestor can do nothing; here the point is that nobody can do anything with him, so the English departs, taking the passive sense of ἀμήχανα ἔργα ‘deeds past help’ at 8.130. γεραιέ is the vocative again. The unit begins in the middle of line 167.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The formula of the speaker who answers in turn, as at 119, with Nestor’s name-epithet: τόν ‘him’ is Diomedes, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπε the Homeric form of ‘addressed’. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα φίλος κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: nai dē tauta ge panta philos kata moiran eeipes.
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, all this, dear friend, according to what is fitting you have said.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, my friend, you have said all this as is fitting.
sentences.n: ναὶ δή is ‘yes indeed’, and ταῦτά γε πάντα ‘all this’, with γε stressing it. φίλος is the vocative of φίλος ‘dear’, ‘my friend’. κατὰ μοῖραν ‘according to what is fitting’ is a phrase of the Odyssey, whose English is kept; ἔειπες is the epic aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t:
εἰσὶν μέν μοι παῖδες ἀμύμονες, εἰσὶ δὲ λαοὶ
καὶ πολέες, τῶν κέν τις ἐποιχόμενος καλέσειεν·
sentences.tr:
eisin men moi paides amymones, eisi de laoi
kai polees, tōn ken tis epoichomenos kaleseien·
sentences.l:
There are, indeed, for me sons, blameless, and there are people
also many, of whom someone, going about, might call them;
sentences.i: I have sons who are blameless, and many men as well, any of whom might go about and call them;
sentences.n: εἰσὶν μέν μοι ‘there are for me’, that is, ‘I have’; the μέν is answered by ἀλλά in line 172. παῖδες ἀμύμονες ‘blameless sons’: the meaning of ἀμύμων is not known for certain, and ‘blameless’ is the traditional rendering. λαοί are ‘people’, here men under his command, and πολέες is the epic πολλοί. τῶν κέν τις ἐποιχόμενος καλέσειεν ‘any one of whom might go about and call’ is a potential optative with κεν; the verb ἐποίχομαι takes up Diomedes’ words, and ‘them’, the kings, is understood.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μάλα μεγάλη χρειὼ βεβίηκεν Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr: alla mala megalē chreiō bebiēken Achaious.
sentences.l: but a very great need has come upon the Achaeans.
sentences.i: but a very great need has come upon the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἀλλά gives the reason why even such help is not enough. μάλα μεγάλη χρειώ ‘a very great need’ is the subject, and βεβίηκεν is the verb of line 145, ‘has come upon’, the sense not quite certain.

sentences.t:
νῦν γὰρ δὴ πάντεσσιν ἐπὶ ξυροῦ ἵσταται ἀκμῆς
ἢ μάλα λυγρὸς ὄλεθρος Ἀχαιοῖς ἠὲ βιῶναι.
sentences.tr:
nyn gar dē pantessin epi xyrou histatai akmēs
ē mala lygros olethros Achaiois ēe biōnai.
sentences.l:
For now indeed, for all, it stands on a razor’s edge:
either very grievous destruction for the Achaeans, or to live.
sentences.i: For now it stands on a razor’s edge for all of us: either very grievous destruction for the Achaeans, or to live.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ ξυροῦ ἵσταται ἀκμῆς ‘it stands on the edge of a razor’: ξυρόν is a razor and ἀκμή its sharp edge, a picture of a point of crisis. πάντεσσιν ‘for all’ is the epic dative plural, and the subject of ἵσταται, the issue, is not stated. The choice follows: ἢ … ἠέ ‘either … or’, μάλα λυγρὸς ὄλεθρος Ἀχαιοῖς ‘very grievous destruction for the Achaeans’ (the verb ‘is’ understood), and βιῶναι ‘to live’, the aorist infinitive of βιόω.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν Αἴαντα ταχὺν καὶ Φυλέος υἱὸν
ἄνστησον·
sentences.tr:
all’ ithi nyn Aianta tachyn kai Phyleos huion
anstēson·
sentences.l:
But go now, swift Ajax and the son of Phyleus
rouse up;
sentences.i: But go now and rouse swift Ajax and the son of Phyleus;
sentences.n: ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’; ἄνστησον is the aorist imperative of ἀνίστημι ‘make stand up, rouse’, and its two objects, Αἴαντα ταχύν and Φυλέος υἱόν, are the ones Nestor named at 110, the second again unnamed. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 176.

sentences.t: σὺ γάρ ἐσσι νεώτερος·
sentences.tr: sy gar essi neōteros·
sentences.l: for you are younger;
sentences.i: for you are the younger man;
sentences.n: σὺ γάρ gives the reason why Diomedes is sent: νεώτερος is the comparative of νέος ‘young’, ‘younger’ than Nestor. The unit ends at the raised dot (·).

sentences.t: εἴ μ’ ἐλεαίρεις.
sentences.tr: ei m’ eleaireis.
sentences.l: if you pity me.”
sentences.i: if you have pity on me.”
sentences.n: εἴ μ’ ἐλεαίρεις ‘if you pity me’ is a plea in the form of a condition left without an answer. ἐλεαίρω is ‘pity’. Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἑέσσατο δέρμα λέοντος
αἴθωνος μεγάλοιο ποδηνεκές, εἵλετο δ’ ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho d’ amph’ ōmoisin heessato derma leontos
aithōnos megaloio podēnekes, heileto d’ enchos.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he about his shoulders put on the skin of a lion,
tawny, great, reaching to the feet, and he took a spear.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and put the skin of a great tawny lion about his shoulders, reaching to his feet, and took a spear.
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins, and Diomedes arms. Line 178 stands word for word at 10.24, where Agamemnon put on his lion skin. ἑέσσατο is the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe oneself in’; ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ‘about his shoulders’. δέρμα λέοντος ‘the skin of a lion’ is followed by αἴθωνος ‘tawny’, μεγάλοιο ‘great’ and ποδηνεκές ‘reaching to the feet’, which agrees with δέρμα. εἵλετο δ’ ἔγχος ‘and he took a spear’.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, τοὺς δ’ ἔνθεν ἀναστήσας ἄγεν ἥρως.
sentences.tr: bē d’ ienai, tous d’ enthen anastēsas agen hērōs.
sentences.l: and he set out to go, and those from there, having roused them, he led, the hero.
sentences.i: He set out, and having roused them from there the hero led them along.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι ‘set out to go’, as at 136. τοὺς δ’ ἔνθεν ἀναστήσας ἄγεν ἥρως: τούς are the men Nestor told him to rouse at 175, ἔνθεν ‘from there’, ἀναστήσας the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, and ἄγεν the imperfect of ἄγω without augment. ἥρως ‘the hero’ is Diomedes, as at 154.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ φυλάκεσσιν ἐν ἀγρομένοισιν ἔμιχθεν,
οὐδὲ μὲν εὕδοντας φυλάκων ἡγήτορας εὗρον,
ἀλλ’ ἐγρηγορτὶ σὺν τεύχεσιν εἵατο πάντες.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē phylakessin en agromenoisin emichthen,
oude men heudontas phylakōn hēgētoras heuron,
all’ egrēgorti syn teuchesin heiato pantes.
sentences.l:
And when they were mingled among the guards, who were assembled,
nor indeed sleeping the leaders of the guards did they find,
but awake, with armour, they sat, all of them.
sentences.i: And when they came among the guards, who had gathered, they did not find the leaders of the guards sleeping, but all of them sitting awake in their armour.
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins, and the party reaches the guards. οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ‘and when they’; ἐν … ἔμιχθεν is a tmesis, ‘were mingled among’, the aorist passive of μίγνυμι with the dative φυλάκεσσιν. ἀγρομένοισιν is a shortened aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω, ‘assembled’. οὐδὲ μέν … εὕδοντας ‘nor indeed sleeping’, the participle of εὕδω agreeing with φυλάκων ἡγήτορας ‘the leaders of the guards’. ἐγρηγορτί is an adverb ‘awake’, from the perfect of ἐγείρω; σὺν τεύχεσιν ‘in armour’; εἵατο is the epic third plural imperfect of ἧμαι, ‘were sitting’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ κύνες περὶ μῆλα δυσωρήσωνται ἐν αὐλῇ
θηρὸς ἀκούσαντες κρατερόφρονος, ὅς τε καθ’ ὕλην
ἔρχηται δι’ ὄρεσφι·
sentences.tr:
hōs de kynes peri mēla dysōrēsōntai en aulēi
thēros akousantes kraterophronos, hos te kath’ hylēn
erchētai di’ oresphi·
sentences.i: As dogs keep a troubled watch around the flocks in the fold when they have heard a beast of strong mind that comes through the forest, through the mountains;
sentences.n: A simile: ὡς δέ ‘and as’. The subjunctive δυσωρήσωνται, with no κε, is the ordinary epic subjunctive of a simile; δυσωρέω is a rare verb, taken to mean ‘keep a troubled watch’, and its formation is not certain. περὶ μῆλα ‘around the flocks’, ἐν αὐλῇ ‘in the fold’ (αὐλή ‘farmyard, enclosure’). θηρὸς ἀκούσαντες ‘having heard a wild beast’, with the genitive of what is heard; κρατερόφρονος ‘strong-minded’. ὅς τε … ἔρχηται ‘which comes’, the relative with epic τε and a subjunctive for what happens at times. καθ’ ὕλην ‘through the forest’; ὄρεσφι has the ending -φι, ‘through the mountains’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 185.

sentences.t:
πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ κυνῶν, ἀπό τέ σφισιν ὕπνος ὄλωλεν·
sentences.tr:
polys d’ orymagdos ep’ autōi
andrōn ēde kynōn, apo te sphisin hypnos olōlen·
sentences.l:
and a great din is upon it
of men and dogs, and from them sleep has perished;
sentences.i: and a great din is raised at it by men and dogs, and sleep is gone from them;
sentences.n: πολὺς δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸς ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘and a great din upon it’: ὀρυμαγδός is ‘din’, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘at it’, that is, at the beast, and the verb ‘is raised’ is left out. ἀνδρῶν ἠδὲ κυνῶν ‘of men and dogs’ says who makes the din. ἀπό τέ σφισιν ὕπνος ὄλωλεν ‘and from them sleep has perished’ has a tmesis (ἀπό … ὄλωλεν); ὄλωλεν is the perfect of ὄλλυμι with the sense ‘is gone’, and σφισιν is ‘for them’. The unit begins in the middle of line 185.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν νήδυμος ὕπνος ἀπὸ βλεφάροιιν ὀλώλει
νύκτα φυλασσομένοισι κακήν·
sentences.tr:
hōs tōn nēdymos hypnos apo blepharoiin olōlei
nykta phylassomenoisi kakēn·
sentences.l:
so from them sweet sleep from their eyelids had perished,
as they kept watch through the evil night;
sentences.i: so sweet sleep was gone from their eyelids as they kept watch through the evil night;
sentences.n: ὣς τῶν … ὀλώλει is the other half of the simile: ‘so for them sleep had perished’. ὀλώλει is the pluperfect of ὄλλυμι, ‘was gone’, with a tmesis (ἀπὸ … ὀλώλει); τῶν is ‘from them’, the guards, and βλεφάροιιν is a dual genitive, ‘from the two eyelids’. νήδυμος ὕπνος ‘sweet sleep’: the meaning of νήδυμος is not known, and ‘sweet’ is traditional (see line 91). φυλασσομένοισι is a dative plural participle, ‘as they kept watch’, and νύκτα … κακήν ‘through the evil night’ is an accusative of time. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 188.

sentences.t:
πεδίον δὲ γὰρ αἰεὶ
τετράφαθ’, ὁππότ’ ἐπὶ Τρώων ἀΐοιεν ἰόντων.
sentences.tr:
pedion de gar aiei
tetraphath’, hoppot’ epi Trōōn aïoien iontōn.
sentences.l:
for toward the plain always
they had turned, whenever they heard the Trojans coming on.
sentences.i: for they were always turned toward the plain, whenever they heard the Trojans coming on.
sentences.n: πεδίον δὲ γὰρ αἰεί: the plain is the goal of τετράφαθ’, which is τετράφατο, the pluperfect passive third plural of τρέπω, ‘had turned (themselves)’. ὁππότ’ ἐπὶ Τρώων ἀΐοιεν ἰόντων ‘whenever they heard the Trojans coming on’: ὁππότε with the optative marks repetition in the past, ἀΐοιεν is the optative of ἀΐω ‘perceive, hear’, and it takes the genitive Τρώων ἰόντων. ἐπί may go with ἰόντων, ‘coming against’. The unit begins in the middle of line 188.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ὃ γέρων γήθησεν ἰδὼν θάρσυνέ τε μύθῳ
καί σφεας φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ ho gerōn gēthēsen idōn tharsyne te mythōi
kai spheas phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And at them the old man rejoiced, seeing, and cheered them with a word,
and, lifting his voice, to them winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: The old man rejoiced when he saw them, and cheered them with a word, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ ὃ γέρων: τούς ‘them’ is the object of ἰδών ‘seeing’, and ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ is Nestor. γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’; θάρσυνε is the aorist of θαρσύνω ‘cheer, encourage’, and μύθῳ ‘with a word’ is a dative of means. Line 191 is the formula that also stands at 4.284, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: οὕτω νῦν φίλα τέκνα φυλάσσετε·
sentences.tr: houtō nyn phila tekna phylassete·
sentences.l: “Thus now, dear children, keep watch;
sentences.i: “Keep watch like this now, dear children;
sentences.n: Nestor speaks to the guards. οὕτω νῦν ‘so now’; φίλα τέκνα ‘dear children’, with φίλα neuter plural agreeing with τέκνα; φυλάσσετε is the present imperative of φυλάσσω ‘keep watch’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·), in the middle of line 192.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τιν’ ὕπνος
αἱρείτω, μὴ χάρμα γενώμεθα δυσμενέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
mēde tin’ hypnos
haireitō, mē charma genōmetha dysmeneessin.
sentences.l:
and let not sleep take any one,
lest we become a joy to the ill-disposed.”
sentences.i: and let sleep not take any one of you, lest we become a joy to the ill-disposed.”
sentences.n: μηδέ τιν’ ὕπνος αἱρείτω ‘and let not sleep take any one’: αἱρείτω is the third singular imperative of αἱρέω ‘take, seize’, with the object τιν’ before the subject ὕπνος. μὴ … γενώμεθα is a subjunctive after μή, ‘lest we become’. χάρμα is ‘a joy’, a cause for rejoicing, as in the Odyssey, and δυσμενέεσσιν ‘to the ill-disposed’ is the dative plural, the Trojans. Nestor’s speech, and the part, end here.
